messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 71
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Forensic Analyst
- Trauma Type: Assault
- Pcl5: 61

Mrs. D., a 71-year-old forensic analyst, still works three days a week at the regional crime lab, though she has not processed a single piece of evidence from a violent crime in the past eight months. She used to love the puzzle of it—the way a single hair, a grain of soil, a smudge of blood could tell a story. Now the story she sees is only her own.

It happened eighteen months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late October. She had stayed late at the lab to finish a complex ballistics report, and the parking garage was nearly empty. As she reached her car, a man came up behind her. He pressed something hard into her back—she still doesn’t know if it was a gun or a knife—and forced her into the passenger seat. He drove her to an abandoned warehouse on the edge of town. She remembers the cold of the concrete floor, the smell of rust and diesel. He told her not to look at him, but she saw his boots: black work boots with a distinctive scuff mark on the right toe. He tied her hands with a phone cord he had in his pocket. He took her wallet, her phone, her wedding ring. Then he left. She managed to free herself after an hour and walked to a gas station three miles away.

The police caught him six weeks later. She identified his boots in a lineup. That part felt like justice. But the rest of it—the part that lives inside her—has never been sentenced.

In the months after the assault, Mrs. D. stopped sleeping. She would lie next to her husband, Frank, staring at the ceiling, her heart pounding at every creak of the house. She began to avoid the parking garage at work. She takes the bus now, even though it adds forty minutes to her commute and Frank has offered to drive her every day. She cannot explain why the bus feels safer—it does not. The seats are too close, the sudden stops make her flinch, and any man in work boots triggers a cold sweat. But at least the bus has other people. The garage is empty, and emptiness now feels like a trap.

Her work has become a minefield. She used to examine crime scene photographs with clinical detachment. Now, when she sees a picture of a ligature mark, she feels the phone cord around her own wrists. When a detective describes a victim’s fear, she feels her own throat tighten. She has begun requesting only property crimes and fraud cases—anything without a person in it. Her supervisor has noticed. Mrs. D. told him she was “slowing down” with age, but she knows it is not age. It is the way her mind replays the warehouse scene in perfect, unwanted clarity: the echo of his footsteps, the scrape of the cord, the weight of her ring being pulled off.

She has also become what her daughter calls “a security fanatic.” She checks the locks on every door three times before bed. She refuses to answer the phone if the number is unknown. She keeps a small can of pepper spray in her purse, in her coat pocket, and on the nightstand. Frank has tried to be patient, but last week he said, “Honey, he’s in prison. He can’t hurt you.” She looked at him and said, “I know.” But the part of her that knows does not reach the part of her that feels.

Last month, at the grocery store, a stranger tapped her on the shoulder to ask for the salt. She spun around so fast she knocked a jar of pasta sauce off the shelf. It shattered on the floor. She started shaking and could not stop. The store manager brought her a chair and a glass of water. She told him she was fine, but she was not fine. She left the cart full of groceries and walked home.

She has not told Frank about the nightmares—the ones where she is back in the warehouse, but this time he does not leave. She wakes gasping, the sheets twisted around her legs like the phone cord. Some mornings she lies in bed until Frank leaves for work, too exhausted to face the day, too ashamed to explain why.

Yesterday, during a routine staff meeting, a young analyst presented a case involving a home invasion. Mrs. D. sat at the back of the room, her hands clammy, her vision tunneling. She heard the word “restrained” and felt her throat close. She excused herself to the bathroom and vomited. She stood at the sink, looking at her own face in the mirror—the same face she saw in the rearview mirror that night, trying not to cry because he had told her not to make a sound. She is a forensic analyst, a woman who has built a career on examining the details of violence from a safe distance. But the distance is gone now. The violence is inside her, and it has taken up permanent residence.
